1:
The title is where the commentators begin, and where they divide. Henry calls it very observable and reads the psalm as composed by one afflicted with the church and for it, and calculated for others in like distress, the Holy Ghost having drawn up the petition and put words into our mouths. Clarke reports that the Hebrew and nearly all the versions carry the same heading, takes the psalm as the prayer of the captives in Babylon near the end of their oppression, and notes that the apostle applies three of its later verses to Christ. Calvin agrees on the setting but argues a date: not after the return, when the rebuilding was hindered, but before it, when deliverance was at hand and the prophets were beginning to lift up the hearts of the godly. He also insists on who may use it: the form was prescribed only to those distressed at the Church's desolation, and no man could utter the words without profaning God's name unless sincere affection moved him.

Calvin turns the title into an argument about prayer itself. He notes that some take the verb for being overwhelmed as a figure for a man too grieved to lift his face, and finds instead a play on words: when grief so shuts us up that we shun the presence of men, the gate is so far from being shut against our prayers that this is the properest season for them. He adds a rebuke to his own readers, that while each man takes care of his own interests, scarcely one in a hundred is affected as he ought by the calamities of the Church.

Augustine asks who the poor man praying here is, answering from the apostle that he was rich and for our sakes became poor. He develops the riches, first the common ones of ability, memory, health and the senses, by which even the poor are rich, then the greater ones of faith, piety and charity, which no man has except through him who justifies the ungodly; and he asks how one so rich can be found eating ashes for bread, answering that he took our poverty when clothed in the form of a servant, lest we should dread his riches.

Delitzsch treats the opening verses as unoriginal by design: they are familiar expressions of prayer, the kind that rise in the heart of the praying man without his feeling them to be of foreign origin, and he lists half a dozen psalms from which each phrase might be drawn; only from the third verse does the psalm become original. Ellicott says the same, that prayer like love has its own language and takes here the forms that meet us elsewhere. Spurgeon reads the plea for a hearing as the whole substance: it is a relief to acquaint others with our trouble, but the sweetest solace is God himself as a sympathizing listener, and we might as well be atheists as believe in an unfeeling God.

On the images of wasting the readings are close but not identical. Delitzsch takes the bones as heated with fever as a hearth is with its fire, and reports a variant that would enrich the lexicon with a word that has scarcely existed. Ellicott prefers brand or fuel to hearth. Clarke turns the whole into an allegory of the captivity, the psalmist a pile of combustible matter on a fire, part flying away as smoke and the rest left as charred coal, the Chaldeans being the fire and the Jews the fuel; on the withered heart he takes the figure from grass cut in the meadow and withered by the sun. Gill keeps it personal, reading the days consumed in smoke as days spent in the obscurity of affliction; Ellicott corrects the next clause to say the psalmist has forgotten to eat rather than that he is prevented.
5:
The birds draw the most work. Gill offers two etymologies for the first, from its smiting its own breast to revive its young and from its vomiting up shellfish, and settles on a bird of solitude, reporting an ancient identification of it as an Egyptian bird of the Nile desert. Clarke allows the pelican or the bittern for the first, and some owl for the second. Ellicott answers the standing objection that a pelican is a water-bird and would starve in a desert: the Hebrew word covers any wide open space, and the pelican does retire far inland after filling its pouch; the bird sitting with its bill on its breast is, he adds, a true picture of the complaint. On the second bird he reports that the Hebrew identifies it as an owl and should be rendered owl of the ruins, notes that some make it a pelican again since the word means cup, and lists versions giving screech-owl and hoopoe. Wesley notes only that a pelican is solitary and mournful.

On the lonely bird of the next verse the uncertainty recurs. Clarke says the word seems often used of any small bird, and reports a proposal that the screech owl is meant; Ellicott renders it a lonely bird, notes a manuscript reading making it wandering, and glosses the watching as sleeplessness.

The enemies produce a disagreement about a single phrase. Clarke takes the swearing as the Chaldeans binding themselves by oath to destroy the captives, and compares the Jews who swore not to eat until they had killed Paul. Ellicott corrects the preposition: they do not swear against him but by him, making his name a byword of execration, though the Greek and Latin read it the other way. Gill keeps it general: good men always have enemies who are also enemies to God, and reproach for religion should be reckoned greater riches than the treasures of Egypt.

Ashes for bread is read both ways. Delitzsch takes it plainly, the mourner sitting in ashes and throwing them over himself, so that ashes are his bread. Gill adds a second construction, that the words may be inverted so that he ate bread like ashes, relishing it no more than if it were ashes, the bread of adversity. Wesley makes the ashes as familiar as bread, the mourner covering his head with them and lying down in them. Ellicott treats the phrase as figurative, comparing the serpent's dust for meat, and sets beside it a modern poet on food that fell to dust as it was eaten.

The lifting up and casting down is agreed in sense and differently pictured. Delitzsch reads God first taking away the firm ground from under the man's feet and then casting him down from aloft, an emblem of Israel removed from its fatherland into exile. Clarke makes it one motion, lifted on high that he might be dashed down with greater force, and applies it to a people once exalted in God's favour and now the most abject. Ellicott sees a whirlwind. Gill turns inward: God's people deserve his wrath as much as others and under afflictions readily conclude they are under it, but this is their apprehension only, since Christ bore it in their stead.

The closing image is corrected by two of them. The English makes the shadow decline; Ellicott renders it a lengthening shadow, growing longer as the day declines and therefore soon to vanish, and quotes Milton for it. Clarke reads the days as declining like the shadow rather than the shadow declining, sees an allusion to the sun's southward turn, and matches it with a contemporary prophet's cry that the harvest is past and the summer ended. Gill notes that a life reckoned by days is compared to a shadow because it has no substance, and reports the Greek poet who called man the dream of a shadow.
12:
The turn is felt as a deliberate reversal. Henry sets it against the complaint: our life is transient but God's permanent, our names written in dust but his remembrance to all generations, and a good man loves God better than himself and can balance his own death against the blessedness of the Eternal Mind. Spurgeon notes that the Hebrew word is sit, so God is enthroned to eternity, and finds the consolation in sovereignty: he reigns whatever happens, his throne secure though the chosen city lies in ruins. Ellicott makes God's eternity a pledge of the national hopes, and he and Wesley both gloss the remembrance from the divine name given at the bush, itself called God's memorial to all generations. Gill alone addresses the verse to Christ, arguing from the New Testament use of it. Delitzsch reads it as the promise's guarantee: when the church dies off member by member on foreign soil, the unchangeable God remains.

The set time for mercy on Zion is read as fixed, not merely expected. Henry says the encouraging thing is that a time is set, which will come not merely some day but at the day Infinite Wisdom appointed, and therefore the best day. Clarke identifies it as Jeremiah's seventy years, now ended. Gill declines the exilic reading and refers it to the restoring of the church in the latter day.

The stones and dust of the ruin draw the warmest writing. Henry observes that though the temple was ruined its stones were still to be had for a new building, and that those who truly love the church love it in affliction as well as prosperity. Clarke says the rubbish was sacred in pious eyes as the city of the great King. Ellicott illustrates it from the history of the rebuilding and from the wailing place in modern Jerusalem. Gill again refuses the historical reference and makes the stones the converts of the latter day.

On the heathen fearing as a result, Delitzsch places the argument's weight. He notes that the fulfilment is urged upon God because his own honour depends on it, the restoration of Jerusalem becoming the means of the world's conversion, and hears in the strophe a lyric echo of the prophecy that the restoration and the coming of the Lord will happen together. Ellicott notes that this result occupies a great prophecy. Clarke instead traces the steps by which the Gentile world was prepared, the edict of Cyrus, the translation of the Scriptures into Greek, and the dispersion of the Jews through the Roman empire.

The prayer of the destitute has its philology worked over. Clarke renders it of one laid in utter ruin and entirely wasted. Ellicott gives it literally as the naked one, the exiles stripped of home and rites, and notes that the word occurs only once more in Scripture, where it is rendered heath, and is still the Arabic name of a stunted Palestinian bush. Henry calls it an elegant word for the low shrub of the wilderness, and takes it either of a broken outward state or of the broken spirit God looks for, adding that God will not merely regard such prayer but value it. Gill applies it to the church under antichrist.

On the writing down for a later generation Ellicott notices what the others do not: this is the only place in the psalms where the memory of great events is said to be preserved in writing rather than orally. Delitzsch calls what is written the evangel of God's redemptive deed and the people to be created the church of the future; Clarke identifies them as the Gentiles brought to salvation. Henry, on the prisoners, notes that God hears not only prayers, the language of grace, but groans, the language of nature; Gill applies the prison to the inquisition, Clarke to the whole race under sentence of death.
23:
Whose strength is weakened is the first question. Ellicott takes the phrase as in the course of life, notes an alternative rendering, and says the meaning is the same. Gill insists the weakener is God and not the enemy, and reads the afflictions as those every believer meets. Henry takes it corporately: the Jewish church was in danger of being cut off, having been for ages on the way to the promise of the Messiah; when the ten tribes were lost in Assyria and the two almost lost in Babylon its strength was weakened, and if these fail the promise fails. Wesley records that some take the psalmist to speak of the whole commonwealth as of one man. He then applies it to the individual under two afflictions, sickness and a short life, adding that it has often been the lot of those who used their strength well to have it weakened, and of those who could ill be spared to have their days shortened.

The prayer that follows is read the same two ways. Henry makes it the church pleading not to be cut off before the Messiah comes, since the blessing is in her; Wesley says the same in a line. Clarke takes it as the form of prayer the captives used before deliverance, and notes that the argument from our frailty against God's permanence was often used to induce him to hear. Ellicott grounds it in the fear of not living to see the restoration of his race. Gill notes that dying in the midst of one's days was reckoned a token of displeasure, the Hebrew saying rather cause me not to ascend.

On the eternity that answers the prayer Henry defers to the apostle: these verses are quoted in the epistle and said there to be spoken to the Son, and in that exposition we must acquiesce. God made the world and therefore was before it, and will unmake it and therefore will be after it. Gill reads the founding of the earth as proof of Christ's deity and as confuting the notion of an eternal world, and offers a rendering that makes the divine years prior to the founding itself. Clarke agrees that no one taught of God ever imagined the world eternal, and insists the earth did not grow by accretion from a pre-existent nucleus.

How the heavens and earth perish divides them. Gill says it is not as to substance but as to quality, reporting a grammarian who put it as not in their generals but their particulars. Henry takes the change as a laying aside rather than a gradual decay, like an old garment no longer needed, altered and not annihilated. Clarke argues from necessity: what is not eternal must be perishable, and he finds the evidence in universal deterioration, since the same seed planted several years running degenerates until it is not worth tillage however the soil is manured, instancing wheat and the potato. Ellicott takes the fixed earth and uplifted mountains as symbols of endurance beside man but a wearing vesture beside God, and follows the image through the lines about weaving at the roaring loom of time the garment God is seen by, into a later writer's philosophy of clothes; geology confirms the figure, he adds, time stripping the robe off the hills to fold it down at a river mouth.

The last verse turns on one word. Ellicott corrects continue to dwell, meaning in the land. Gill takes the servants for the ministers of the word and their children for those begotten through the Gospel. Clarke says the Church is permanent, being founded on God. Henry draws the inference the psalm has been building: since Christ is the same the church continues, and from the eternity of the head we infer the perpetuity of the body, so those who hope to wear out the saints will be mistaken.
